articles.title: Littleborough defeat Trafford MV in ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 clash
articles.excerpt: Littleborough secured a victory against Trafford MV, maintaining their position at the top of ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 despite challenging weather conditions.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough Rugby Club faced Trafford MV in a challenging match in the ADM Lancs/Cheshire 2 league on Saturday, October 26, 2026. The match took place at Littleborough's home ground, where the team managed to secure a win despite adverse weather conditions, including heavy rain and strong winds.

Trafford MV entered the game with a number of key players unavailable due to injuries, which affected their performance. They initially took the lead with a try from Mica Dyos, making the score 5-0. However, Littleborough responded quickly, scoring a try and converting it to lead 7-5 at half-time.

In the second half, Littleborough capitalised on the weather and the slope of the pitch, scoring another try and a penalty to extend their lead to 15-7. They added a further try, bringing the score to 22-7, before Trafford MV managed to score again through Aaron Booth, who converted his own try, reducing the deficit to 22-12.

This victory keeps Littleborough at the top of the league, while Trafford MV slips further down the standings. The match highlights the challenges teams face during adverse weather conditions and the impact of player availability on performance.

articles.title: Free benefits checks at Littleborough and Wardle libraries on Monday and Tuesday
articles.excerpt: Council advisers will offer free, no booking needed benefits checks at Littleborough Library on 26 October and Wardle Library on 27 October, from 10am to noon.
articles.content_html:
Residents unsure whether they are receiving all the financial support available to them can speak to council advisers at two free library drop in sessions this week. The sessions are particularly relevant to pensioners, carers, disabled residents and people worried about household costs, but the council says they are open to adults generally.

The first is at Littleborough Library in Hare Hill Park, Littleborough OL15 9HE, on Monday 26 October 2026 from 10am until noon. The second takes place at Wardle Library, 448 Birch Road, Wardle OL12 9LH, on Tuesday 27 October, also from 10am until noon. No appointment is needed for either event.

The council says advisers can check potential entitlement to Pension Credit, explain Attendance Allowance, review Council Tax Support eligibility and give information about Winter Fuel Payments, Blue Badge applications and other cost of living assistance. They can also signpost residents to organisations offering further help, including Citizens Advice and Age UK. Attending does not guarantee entitlement to a benefit or an immediate payment: decisions depend on the relevant eligibility rules and application process.

Anyone attending is asked to bring details of their income, pensions, savings and benefits already received, so advisers can offer a more accurate check. Those visiting on behalf of a family member should bring relevant information if available. Take care with personal documents and give sensitive details only to the advisers at the official session.

Both sessions are advertised by Rochdale Borough Council as free and do not require booking. Anyone unable to attend can use the council's published events information to find its contact details and check for other advice sessions.

Official event details: Littleborough Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1484/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---littleborough-library and Wardle Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1485/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---wardle-library.

articles.title: New documentary explores the history of Hollingworth Lake
articles.excerpt: A new YouTube documentary delves into the fascinating history of Hollingworth Lake, revealing its origins and significance to the local community.
articles.content_html:
Hollingworth Lake, a popular recreational area for residents of Oldham, Rochdale, and surrounding regions, has been the subject of a new YouTube documentary that explores its intriguing history. Created by Malc Grimwood, a local history enthusiast, the documentary is part of his channel "Tales From Trails Around The Dales."

The lake, situated on the outskirts of Littleborough beneath the Pennine hills, is a man-made body of water that was established during the Industrial Revolution to support the extensive canal network. Grimwood highlights the lake's significance, stating, "Hollingworth Lake is one of Rochdale's most cherished and well-known beauty spots, offering an escape and a place to enjoy its open spaces and rural setting."

The documentary not only sheds light on the lake's origins but also aims to connect viewers with the natural beauty and historical context of the area. It showcases the surrounding countryside, wooded slopes, and moorland that contribute to the lake's charm and appeal.

For those interested in local history and the environment, the documentary serves as an engaging resource. It invites viewers to appreciate the rich heritage of Hollingworth Lake and encourages them to explore the area, fostering a deeper connection with this beloved landmark.

articles.title: Roadworks scheduled on Kirkstall Avenue in Littleborough on 6 November 2026
articles.excerpt: Kirkstall Avenue in Littleborough will be temporarily closed for roadworks starting on 6 November 2026, affecting local traffic and access.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that part of Kirkstall Avenue in Littleborough will be temporarily closed for roadworks on 6 November 2026. The closure will extend from 34 metres past the junction with Tintern Avenue and will end 23 metres further down the road in a south-westerly direction.

During this period, no waiting will be allowed in the closed section of the road. This closure may impact local traffic and access to nearby roads, including Shore Road, Furness Avenue, and Tintern Avenue.

Residents and motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly and consider alternative routes during the roadworks. The council has provided a map of the roadworks and restrictions across Greater Manchester for further reference.

For the latest updates and to view the map of roadworks, visit the Rochdale Borough Council website. This information is crucial for local residents and commuters to avoid delays and ensure smooth travel during the construction period.

articles.title: Inspector rejects garden fence appeal on Town House Road, Littleborough
articles.excerpt: A planning inspector has upheld Rochdale Council's decision to refuse retrospective planning permission for a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough, citing its negative impact on the area's character.
articles.content_html:
A planning inspector has ruled against a homeowner's appeal regarding a garden fence at 19 Town House Road, Littleborough. Caterina Buonocore had sought retrospective planning permission for a 1.55-metre high boundary fence, which is approximately twice the height of the original fence. The council had previously rejected her application, leading to the appeal.

In the inspector's decision, it was stated that the main concern was the fence's effect on the character and appearance of the area. The inspector noted that boundary treatments in the locality are typically low-level and visually permeable, contributing to a sense of openness and allowing the greenery in front gardens to be appreciated. The inspector remarked that the existing vegetation helps to soften the street scene, enhancing the area's character.

The inspector further explained that the close-boarded timber fence introduced by the appeal contrasts sharply with the more traditional forms of boundary treatment found in the neighbourhood. Observations made on-site indicated that, due to the prominent corner location, the fence appeared particularly stark and incongruous against the backdrop of traditional stone terraces with lower boundary treatments.

As a result of this ruling, Buonocore may now be required to remove the fence, which could have implications for her property and the surrounding area. The decision underscores the importance of maintaining the character of local neighbourhoods and adhering to planning regulations.

articles.title: Rochdale Council addresses concerns over local pub closures
articles.excerpt: Councillor Richard Jackson has raised concerns about the future of local pubs in Littleborough after the closure of The Wheatsheaf, highlighting restrictive covenants that hinder reopening efforts.
articles.content_html:
The future of local pubs in Littleborough is under scrutiny following the recent closure of The Wheatsheaf. This closure has sparked community outcry and raised concerns about the viability of pubs in the area. Councillor Richard Jackson addressed these issues during a Rochdale council meeting on October 15, highlighting the challenges posed by restrictive covenants that prevent former pubs from being reopened as such.

Councillor Jackson noted that approximately 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies, which often include covenants in sales to deter competition. This practice has led to a significant number of closures, with many pubs being sold off for alternative uses. He cited the example of the former Royal Oak pub, which closed in 2015 and was subsequently converted into a vape shop, a change that was later halted by Trading Standards due to regulatory issues.

The council's discussion aims to address the ongoing loss of pubs in the community, with Jackson's motion seeking to reduce the impact of these covenants. He expressed concern over the cycle of tenant attrition that many pubs face, stating, "We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant."

The implications of this discussion are significant for local residents and pub enthusiasts, as the council considers measures to protect these community assets. The outcome of this motion could influence future policies regarding the sale and repurposing of pubs in Littleborough and beyond.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town hall fears for the future of pubs | Roch Valley Radio On Air Live now — track details aren't available right now Listen Live Watch Town hall fears for the future of pubs George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter October 17, 2026 | 10:55 AM Print Wheatsheaf The Wheatsheaf pub in Littleborough. Is the future of the local pub in danger? That’s the fear in Littleborough where the closure of another pub has sparked outcry. A few months ago The Wheatsheaf closed down in the Rochdalian town. There is strong community interest in reopening the pub as a local asset, but a small loophole means they fear they can’t do that. When breweries or large companies that own and operate pubs sell on the building, they can include a covenant that prevents it from being re-used as a pub. This covenant is inserted into a sale to stop competitors taking the pub on the cheap, the latest town hall meeting was told. Coun Richard Jackson brought forward a motion to Rochdale council to address this very issue to reduce the continued loss of pubs in communities. The Littleborough Lakeside councillor told the chamber on October 15: “The reality is that around 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies. They have a history of damaging the industry as a whole. This often leads to tenant attrition. “We are acutely aware of pubs being closed down after numerous tenants have left the building. The point of this motion is to address the churn. “We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant.” The former Royal Oak pub was closed down in 2015 and then sold off and became a vape shop, which was later shut down by Trading Standards. Coun Jackson called on the council to write to the government to block restrictive covenants on pub sales. He said that this loophole means most pubs get turned into shops or HMOs. His ward colleague Coun Tom Besford shared his annoyance that the future use of a community building can be dictated by the business interests of a brewery or company. The pair also credited Rochdale MP Paul Waugh for his continued work on this issue and raising it in Parliament. Speaking after the motion was passed in Rochdale Town Hall, Mr Waugh said: “This Government has already done the heavy lifting on pubs. Since August, the planning rules make it harder to turn a viable pub into flats or a shop, and the new Community Right to Buy gives people the power to buy their local. But one back door is still wide open. “A pub company can sell up and write into the deeds that the building can never sell another pint, and that ban binds every owner after them. Littleborough lost the Royal Oak that way, and I’m determined that we’re not going to lose the Wheatsheaf too. “The minister has asked for evidence, and with Rochdale council now behind us, I’ll be putting our town’s case to him directly.” It is a tough time for the pub industry nationally, with approximately one pub a day will have closed by the end of 2026, according to the latest figures from the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA).  The trade body estimates that around 360 pubs will permanently shut their doors by the end of the year. articles.title: Volunteers urgently needed at Hollingworth Lake to help Rochdale Sea Cadets
articles.excerpt: GTAS is appealing for volunteers and a donated skip to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets on Saturday 24 October, meeting at 10am.
articles.content_html:
GTAS has issued an urgent appeal for volunteers to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets this Saturday, 24 October.

Anyone able to lend a hand is asked to meet at Hollingworth Lake council car park at 10am. Organisers say help would be welcome for any length of time, whether volunteers can spare an hour or stay for the day.

The group describes the clearance as a big task and is asking people to bring sturdy gardening gloves if they have them. Spades, shovels, loppers, other gardening tools and wheelbarrows would also be useful.

Local businesses are being asked to support the effort too. GTAS is looking for a skip or waste company willing to donate a skip for a few hours to help with the clearance.

The volunteer day is an opportunity for residents and businesses to give practical support to Rochdale Sea Cadets by helping bring the overgrown space back into use.

Anyone who can volunteer or help provide a skip should message GTAS directly through the group’s appeal post.

Could you spare an hour on Saturday, or do you know a business that could help? Share the appeal and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

Source: GTAS community appeal supplied to Rochdale Daily.

Corrections and clarifications

This article was amended on 23 October 2026. Updated following GTAS’s latest appeal. The volunteer meeting is at 10am on Saturday 24 October; the earlier copy gave conflicting dates.

articles.title: Foundry Fields approval includes only five reported social-rent homes among 199 houses
articles.excerpt: Taylor Wimpey’s Foundry Fields scheme received a reported six-to-four committee vote in favour, with one abstention, in January 2026. The 199-home proposal includes detached, semi-detached and terraced houses, with five reported social-rented properties.
articles.content_html:
Taylor Wimpey’s Foundry Fields scheme received a reported six-to-four committee vote in favour, with one abstention, in January 2026. The 199-home proposal includes detached, semi-detached and terraced houses, with five reported social-rented properties.

Five homes amount to approximately 2.5% of the development. This is the reported on-site social-rent figure, not proof that the scheme has no other affordable obligation. The final Section 106 agreement is needed before a definitive statement about its whole affordable package.

The scheme also includes the first phase of a link road between Smithy Bridge Road and Albert Royds Street. A first section should not be described as the completed relief route. Residents need to know which traffic movements it enables before later sections are delivered.

Around half the site is reported as retained for public or open space. School and healthcare capacity still require evidence, and no verified rent schedule or live sales prices were established here.

Taylor Wimpey agreed CMA undertakings in 2021 to remove historic doubling ground-rent terms. Its separate 2025 information-sharing case ended through commitments without an infringement finding. Neither establishes the same issues at Foundry Fields.

The 199 homes belong to the Roch Valley scheme and must not be added to the council’s approximate 200-home allocation as a second development.

Location: West of Smithy Bridge Road, Littleborough; Roch Valley allocation

Planning stage: Committee approval reported January 2026; formal notice/obligations need checking

Homes: 199 homes

Let or for sale: Five social-rent homes reported; remaining tenure and any wider contribution require the final agreement

Land: Greenfield scheme; allocated land formerly within Green Belt

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: No exact future rent, sale price, service charge or estate-charge schedule was established from the council/government material reviewed; no reliable scheme-specific current quotation was identified.

Affordable breakdown: Five on-site social-rent homes reported among 199 (about 2.5%). A verified final schedule establishing any additional cash contribution or affordable tenure was not obtained.

Funded school capacity: The dated Pennines assessment is summarised in the overview. It does not establish Foundry Fields-specific funded school places or an opening date.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: The first section of the Smithy Bridge Road–Albert Royds Street link is included. Full-route completion funding, later phases and additional funded transport-service capacity were not established.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.title: Littleborough’s former AkzoNobel site shows how brownfield housing can include discounted ownership
articles.excerpt: The former AkzoNobel site was announced as a 126-home development through Countryside Partnerships and Together Housing. Its original tenure package included 14 shared-ownership homes and five First Homes, with open-market housing sold under the Bovis brand.
articles.content_html:
The former AkzoNobel site was announced as a 126-home development through Countryside Partnerships and Together Housing. Its original tenure package included 14 shared-ownership homes and five First Homes, with open-market housing sold under the Bovis brand.

That package represents 19 affordable ownership homes, approximately 15.1% of the original total. It should not be described as 19 social-rented properties. Shared ownership also requires scrutiny of rent on the unowned share, service charges and the cost of purchasing additional shares.

The scheme occupies previously developed industrial land bought from Homes England. That distinguishes it from Bloor’s neighbouring farmland proposal. The two developments have separate totals and should be examined together for cumulative traffic, school and healthcare effects.

The announcement’s original delivery dates are now historical. A current assessment needs occupied homes, plots still to build and evidence that remediation conditions have been discharged. Prior industrial use justifies checking contamination evidence; it is not proof that completed homes are unsafe.

Vistry joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

Only remaining future completions belong in a forward housing forecast; houses already occupied cannot be added to the future pipeline again.

Location: Hollingworth Road, Littleborough; former AkzoNobel site

Planning stage: Permission announced in 2023; later material describes construction; remaining delivery requires update

Homes: 126 scheme homes

Let or for sale: 14 shared ownership and five First Homes; remaining homes announced for market sale

Land: Brownfield former industrial site

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: Market housing is sold as Bovis Hollin Bank, but a reproducible current primary-source exact plot quotation was not established in this review. Exact shared-ownership share prices, unowned-share rents, service charges and First Homes prices are not disclosed in the reviewed official/project records.

Affordable breakdown: Announced 126-home mix: 107 market sale, 14 shared ownership and five First Homes. No social-rent homes in that published breakdown. Current delivery and any varied legal schedule are not verified.

Funded school capacity: No site-specific funded school expansion verified. The historical Pennines forecast cannot prove available places for a particular family or cumulative future schemes.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Existing transport access does not establish the remediation/highway conditions have been discharged or that additional services are funded.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.title: Hollingworth Road’s 309 homes: the school land promise needs a delivery explanation
articles.excerpt: Bloor’s Hollingworth Road scheme has been reduced from 312 to 309 homes. Council reporting in June 2026 records site preparation. Developer material includes a central green corridor, sustainable drainage, walking and cycling links and land for a primary school.
articles.content_html:
Bloor’s Hollingworth Road scheme has been reduced from 312 to 309 homes. Council reporting in June 2026 records site preparation. Developer material includes a central green corridor, sustainable drainage, walking and cycling links and land for a primary school.

Pre-decision reporting identifies 47 affordable homes, approximately 15.2% of the scheme. However, its quoted breakdown of 12 social-rent and 25 shared-ownership homes totals only 37. The missing ten must be reconciled against the final affordable schedule before a complete tenure split is published.

The school requires careful explanation. Reporting on the planning assessment says population projections did not then justify immediate delivery. Reserving school land is therefore different from promising that a school will open alongside the first houses. The decision must explain funding, demand thresholds and interim provision.

More than 1,000 objections were reported, including concerns about infrastructure. Bloor identifies transport assessments, drainage measures and replacement visitor parking, but the final conditions and funded works determine what will actually be delivered.

Bloor joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

Location: Hollingworth Road / north of Smithy Bridge, Littleborough

Planning stage: Council June 2026 update records site-preparation work

Homes: 309 revised scheme homes; earlier proposal was 312

Let or for sale: 47 affordable homes reported; social rent/shared ownership envisaged; complete split not reconciled

Land: Farmland / greenfield in an allocated former Green Belt location

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: Bloor’s live Hollingworth Rise page advertises plot 271, a three-bedroom Kane, at £334,995; plot 278, a four-bedroom Locke, at £449,995; and plot 267, a four-bedroom Watercroft, at £489,995. These are market asking prices. Exact social rents and shared-ownership shares, rents and charges are not provided in the reviewed records.

Affordable breakdown: 47 affordable homes reported, comprising 26 two-bedroom, 17 three-bedroom and four four-bedroom dwellings. Published tenure reporting gives 12 social-rent plus 25 shared-ownership homes, only 37: the other ten remain unreconciled. Do not silently change the figures.

Funded school capacity: Land for a potential 420-place primary school is identified. The planning assessment reported no immediate need; an allocated plot is not a funded building. A confirmed budget, operator, demand trigger and opening date were not established.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Drainage, active travel and visitor-parking changes are proposed. Reported contributions exceeding £3 million are not a verified executed item-by-item transport budget, payment record or service-capacity increase.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

Research checked 14 October 2026. Advertised prices are snapshots, not achieved sale prices.

Read the borough-wide housing investigation and the other developments: https://rochdaledaily.co.uk/articles/rochdale-housing-developments-affordability-schools-gp-transport

articles.title: Hollingworth Lake to host Wave of Light walk remembering babies and children
articles.excerpt: Families affected by baby or child loss are invited to meet at Hollingworth Lake's beach at 6.30pm on Thursday 15 October for a remembrance walk and 7pm candle-lighting, with bereavement charities and helplines available for support.
articles.content_html:
Families and friends affected by the death of a baby or child are invited to gather at Hollingworth Lake in Littleborough on Thursday 15 October for a candlelit remembrance walk at the end of Baby Loss Awareness Week.

The community invitation asks people to meet at the beach at Hollingworth Lake at 6.30pm. The group plans to walk together around the lake, pausing approximately halfway round at a scenic point to light candles at 7pm as part of the worldwide Wave of Light.

The invitation is open to anyone who has experienced miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal death, the death of a baby or the loss of a child at any age, as well as relatives, friends, neighbours and others wishing to show their support.

One of the people behind the gathering said that every year they light a candle for the babies they remember. This year, rather than marking the occasion alone, they hope people can come together for a shared moment of remembrance.

Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place each year from 9 to 15 October. At 7pm on 15 October, families around the world take part in the Wave of Light by lighting candles in memory of babies who have died. The Hollingworth Lake walk extends a welcome to those remembering children of all ages.

Those attending can bring a candle or battery-operated light, dress warmly for an October evening and carry a torch for the walk. Please keep a safe distance from the water, take care on paths after dark, never leave flames unattended, and take all candles and materials home rather than leaving them by or in the lake. Details of accessibility arrangements have not been provided in the original invitation.

EVENT DETAILS: Thursday 15 October 2026. Meet at 6.30pm at the beach at Hollingworth Lake, Littleborough, Rochdale, OL15 0AQ. Walk together and stop to light candles at 7pm. This article reports a community invitation; the charities listed below are support resources and are not described as organisers or sponsors of the event.

WHERE TO FIND HELP AFTER BABY OR CHILD LOSS

Grief can affect parents, partners, siblings, grandparents and friends, sometimes long after the death. No one has to attend the walk or speak about a loss to deserve support. The following verified organisations offer specialist information, listening services and, in some cases, counselling or local peer groups.

Sands — confidential help for anyone affected by pregnancy or baby loss, including bereaved relatives and friends. Free national helpline: 0808 164 3332; email: helpline@sands.org.uk; website: https://www.sands.org.uk/support-you/how-we-offer-support/helpline. Telephone hours are Monday to Friday 10am–3pm and Tuesday to Thursday 6pm–9pm, excluding bank holidays.

Child Bereavement UK — support for parents and carers when a baby or child dies, and for bereaved children and young people. Free helpline: 0800 02 888 40, Monday to Friday 8am–8pm, excluding bank holidays. Text or WhatsApp: 07418 341 800 (WhatsApp support for ages 13 and over). Website: https://www.childbereavementuk.org/.

Finding Rainbows — Greater Manchester peer support for families affected by early pregnancy loss or the death of a baby or child. Email: finding.rainbows@outlook.com; website: https://www.findingrainbows.org/.

Tommy's — specialist midwife-led advice on miscarriage, stillbirth, pregnancy after loss and pregnancy-related wellbeing. Free helpline: 0800 0147 800, Monday to Friday 9am–5pm. Email: midwife@tommys.org; website: https://www.tommys.org/. This is a non-urgent advice line.

The Lullaby Trust — specialist bereavement support after the sudden and unexpected death of a baby or young child. Free helpline: 0808 802 6868; website: https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/bereavement-support/find-support/. Phone support is available Monday to Friday 10am–2pm and weekends and public holidays 6pm–10pm.

Antenatal Results and Choices (ARC) — confidential, non-directive support after difficult antenatal test results, fetal diagnosis and pregnancy loss following a decision to end a pregnancy for medical reasons. Helpline: 020 7713 7486, Monday to Friday 10am–5.30pm. Text: 07908 683004; email: info@arc-uk.org; website: https://www.arc-uk.org/.

Miscarriage Association — information and support for anyone affected by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or molar pregnancy. Website: https://www.miscarriageassociation.org.uk/.

Petals — specialist counselling for people affected by pregnancy loss, stillbirth or neonatal death, subject to service eligibility and referral arrangements. Website: https://www.petalscharity.org/.

4Louis — bereavement support resources and memory boxes for families following the death of a baby or child. Website: https://www.4louis.co.uk/.

SUDC UK — information, bereavement support and research relating to sudden unexplained death in childhood. Contact: 07880 350942, Monday to Thursday 9am–5pm; email: info@sudc.org.uk; website: https://sudc.org.uk/.

Greater Manchester NHS PETALS Perinatal Trauma and Loss Service — assessment and therapeutic support for people experiencing trauma related to birth, pregnancy or baby loss. A healthcare professional can make a referral. Telephone: 0161 271 0188 (option 4), Monday to Friday 9am–5pm; website: https://www.gmmh.nhs.uk/petals.

If you need somebody to talk to now, Samaritans offers free emotional support day and night on 116 123 (https://www.samaritans.org/). For urgent mental health support in England, contact NHS 111 and select the mental health option. Call 999 if someone is in immediate danger.

Whatever their age, and however much time has passed, every child deserves to be remembered. Those planning to attend are encouraged to offer one another kindness and space during the gathering.

articles.title: Rochdale’s takeaway winning streak continues as Tandoori Flames takes North West title
articles.excerpt: Littleborough’s Tandoori Flames is the latest Rochdale borough business to take a regional ARTA title, following wins for River Beal in Milnrow and Wild Ginger in Littleborough last year.
articles.content_html:
First Milnrow, now Littleborough. The North West Takeaway of the Year award has found its way to Rochdale borough for the second year running.

Tandoori Flames, on Church Street in Littleborough, won the regional title at the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA), held at the London Hilton on Park Lane on Monday 12 October.

Last year's winner was River Beal Indian Takeaway in Milnrow. And that was not the borough's only success in 2025. Wild Ginger Restaurant in Littleborough also took the North West Restaurant of the Year award.

Three regional awards in two years, all earned by businesses in Littleborough and Milnrow. Not a bad record for the local curry scene.

The 2026 competition attracted more than 1,250 nominations from across the UK. Tandoori Flames and River Beal both appeared on the North West's ten strong takeaway shortlist, alongside businesses from Bolton, Manchester, Wigan and other parts of the region.

Tandoori Flames emerged with the title. The organisers say their judging process considered customer nominations, online reviews, food hygiene ratings and assessments by a panel of judges. That matters because the award is not based on a single enthusiastic recommendation, or merely on how many people happen to vote.

The Littleborough win continues a striking run for neighbouring communities in the borough. River Beal's 2025 title showed that a Milnrow takeaway could compete for regional honours. Wild Ginger's restaurant award in the same year gave Littleborough a victory of its own. Tandoori Flames has now brought another takeaway trophy back to the area.

The ceremony, hosted by presenter Samantha Simmonds and comedian Paul Sinha, brought together restaurateurs and hospitality professionals from around the country. Rochdale MP Paul Waugh was among the guests.

ARTA founder Mohammed Munim congratulated the winners and finalists and drew attention to the rising costs facing independent restaurants. Food, energy and staffing bills have all placed pressure on hospitality businesses, even where customer demand remains strong.

An award does not tell us everything about a restaurant or takeaway. Prices, consistency, service and personal taste still matter to customers. But these results provide a useful measure of how Rochdale businesses are performing beyond the borough.

And there is something pleasing about where the trophies have ended up. The awards cover a region with far larger centres of population and long established dining destinations. Yet, for two years, the takeaway title has gone to addresses in Milnrow and Littleborough.

Rochdale Daily congratulates Tandoori Flames on its 2026 win and recognises the achievements of River Beal and Wild Ginger in 2025.

Have you eaten at any of the three? Tell us what you rate on the menu in the comments. We are always interested in a good local recommendation.

articles.title: Littleborough residents help boost flood resilience through Resilient Roch project
articles.excerpt: Residents at Olive Standring House in Littleborough have joined housing, council and Environment Agency teams to refresh planters while highlighting ongoing flood-resilience work across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Residents at Olive Standring House in Littleborough have been enjoying the summer sunshine while playing a part in efforts to improve flood resilience in the borough.

Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, Rochdale Borough Council, the Environment Agency and contractors joined residents to refresh planters as part of the ongoing Resilient Roch project.

The programme is supporting homes affected by the devastating Boxing Day floods of 2015 as well as properties considered to remain at risk of flooding today.

The work at Olive Standring House provided an opportunity for residents to get involved in improvements to their surroundings while drawing attention to the wider measures being introduced to make homes and communities more resilient to future flooding.

Further improvements are being rolled out across the borough, including flood doors, sump pumps and flood barriers. These measures are intended to reduce the impact on individual properties when extreme rainfall and rising water levels threaten homes.

Littleborough and the wider Pennine area have first-hand experience of the disruption flooding can cause. The Boxing Day floods in 2015 affected communities across the borough and remain an important reference point for current flood-prevention and resilience work.

The Resilient Roch programme brings together housing providers, the council, the Environment Agency, contractors and residents, combining physical protection measures with work intended to help communities prepare for future flood events.

The planter work at Olive Standring House is a smaller but visible part of that wider programme, giving residents an opportunity to participate directly while improvements continue elsewhere across Rochdale borough.

Further information was published by Littleborough Local at https://www.littleboroughlocal.co.uk/2026/08/residents-at-olive-standring-house-help.html.

articles.title: Little'Pink'borough returns as businesses across Littleborough prepare to turn pink for Cancer Research UK
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle are being invited to take part in Little'Pink'borough, a community campaign raising awareness and funds for Cancer Research UK.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough is preparing to turn pink once again as one of the area's colourful community fundraising campaigns returns in eight weeks.

Little'Pink'borough is inviting shops, pubs, clubs, cafés, restaurants, doctors' surgeries, dentists, hairdressers and businesses across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle to get involved in support of Cancer Research UK.

The campaign, organised by The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group, encourages local organisations to create their own pink-themed displays and help transform the area while raising awareness of cancer research.

Businesses are welcome to organise their own fundraising activities as part of the campaign, although organisers stress that in-house fundraising is appreciated rather than essential. Simply taking part and creating a display helps build the community-wide event.

Photographs from previous years are being shared to provide inspiration and get local businesses thinking about what they could create this time around.

There is also a competitive element. The organisation judged to have the best display will receive a bespoke trophy to keep for a year, with the winner's name engraved on it permanently as part of the event's history.

The campaign brings together businesses, community organisations and residents from across the wider Littleborough area around a common cause, while giving streets and shopfronts a distinctive pink makeover.

This year's Little'Pink'borough is being supported by Whittaker Golf Club, which is sponsoring the campaign. The club offers memberships and individual rounds of golf, with further information available through its website.

With eight weeks to go, The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group is encouraging organisations to start planning their displays and decide how they would like to take part.

Further details about the event and fundraising activities are expected as Little'Pink'borough approaches.
articles.right_to_reply: Littleborough, Wardle and Hollingworth Lake businesses taking part in Little'Pink'borough can send photographs, fundraising plans and community updates to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Taxi driver issues safety warning after frightening incident near Littleborough railway station
articles.excerpt: A taxi driver has shared details of a frightening incident near Littleborough railway station in the hope of encouraging colleagues to remain vigilant while waiting for bookings.
articles.content_html:
A taxi driver has urged colleagues across Rochdale borough to remain vigilant after describing a frightening encounter while waiting for his next booking near Littleborough railway station.

The driver said the incident happened shortly after completing an Uber journey from Rochdale Railway Station to a passenger drop-off in Littleborough. After finishing the fare, he parked on a nearby street opposite Littleborough Railway Station while waiting for his next booking.

According to the driver's account, a man described as a white British male aged between 35 and 45 approached the vehicle accompanied by a dog. The driver says the man opened the car door without permission before placing the dog inside the vehicle, along with a bag containing unknown items.

When challenged, the driver alleges the man became aggressive and attempted to damage the vehicle by striking one of the windows. Fearing for his safety, the driver immediately contacted Greater Manchester Police while remaining inside the vehicle.

The driver says the alleged aggression continued while he was speaking to police, prompting him to drive to a safer, busier location near Sainsbury's Local in Littleborough, where he waited for officers to arrive.

Police subsequently attended the scene, took a statement and dealt with the reported incident. Rochdale Daily has approached Greater Manchester Police to establish whether any arrests were made or investigations remain ongoing.

Following the incident, the driver shared his experience publicly in the hope of preventing something similar from happening to others working in the taxi trade.

He is encouraging drivers to avoid waiting for jobs in isolated streets where possible and instead use well-lit locations with passing pedestrians or nearby businesses. He also advises drivers to keep vehicle doors locked while waiting for bookings and to contact police immediately if they feel threatened.

Personal safety is an important consideration for taxi and private hire drivers, many of whom work alone at all hours of the day and night. Drivers frequently find themselves waiting for bookings in unfamiliar locations or transporting passengers they have never previously met. Industry organisations have long encouraged drivers to remain aware of their surroundings, keep communication devices readily available and report suspicious or aggressive behaviour promptly.

While incidents of this nature remain relatively uncommon, they serve as a reminder of the challenges faced by those working in the transport sector. For many drivers, particularly those working evening and overnight shifts, staying alert and choosing safe waiting locations forms an important part of their daily routine.

Anyone who witnesses criminal damage, threatening behaviour or any incident where someone feels at immediate risk should contact Greater Manchester Police on 999 in an emergency, or report non-emergency incidents by calling 101 or using the force's online reporting service.

articles.title: Brass band tradition returns to Hare Hill Park this September
articles.excerpt: Friends of Hare Hill Park are inviting residents to enjoy a free afternoon of brass band music on 6 September, celebrating one of the borough's most treasured historic parks and its long musical tradition.
articles.content_html:
The sound of brass music will once again fill Hare Hill Park this autumn as the Friends of Hare Hill Park invite residents to enjoy an afternoon of live music in one of Rochdale borough's most historic green spaces.

The free concert will take place on Saturday, 6 September, from 3pm until 5pm at the park's historic bandstand, continuing a tradition of open-air performances that has entertained generations of local families. Visitors are encouraged to bring a picnic blanket or folding chair and enjoy an afternoon of music surrounded by the park's award-winning gardens.

The event has been organised by the Friends of Hare Hill Park, a volunteer-led community group established more than 14 years ago to help preserve, improve and promote the Edwardian park. During that time, the group has played a major role in securing funding, restoring historic features and ensuring the park remains one of the borough's best-loved public spaces. Their work has helped attract more than £250,000 towards restoration projects, including improvements to many of the park's original Victorian and Edwardian features. Today, Hare Hill Park proudly holds Green Flag status, recognising it as one of the country's best-managed parks.

Although often associated with Milnrow because of its close proximity, Hare Hill Park actually sits in the heart of neighbouring Littleborough. The park was created during the Victorian era alongside Hare Hill House before the estate was sold to Littleborough Urban District Council in 1900, allowing it to become the public park enjoyed by residents today.

Among its most recognisable landmarks is the Grade II-listed bandstand, presented to the people of Littleborough by local benefactor James Cryer in 1902 to commemorate the coronation of King Edward VII. More than 120 years later, it remains the centrepiece for community concerts and one of the park's most photographed historic features.

Over the decades, Hare Hill Park has welcomed countless visitors, community celebrations and civic events. The grounds have long been a venue for brass band concerts, fêtes, remembrance events, sporting activities and family gatherings, making it one of the social hearts of Littleborough and the surrounding Pennine communities.

Brass banding itself forms an important part of the area's industrial heritage. Mill towns across Lancashire and Greater Manchester developed proud brass band traditions during the nineteenth century, with local bands providing entertainment at parks, public celebrations and civic occasions. That heritage remains alive today, with Milnrow Band—founded in 1869—continuing to enjoy national success, recently earning promotion back to the prestigious British Open Championship following victory at the 2026 Grand Shield competition.

Friends of Hare Hill Park say they hope residents from across Rochdale borough will come along to enjoy an afternoon of live music while supporting the park and the volunteers who work throughout the year to keep it looking its best.

With its beautifully restored bandstand, formal gardens, mature trees and rich history, Hare Hill Park provides an ideal backdrop for a traditional brass band concert. For many visitors, it offers the chance to enjoy not only live music but one of the borough's finest historic parks, whose heritage continues to be protected by a dedicated group of local volunteers.

The concert is free to attend and takes place on Saturday, 6 September, between 3pm and 5pm.

articles.title: Littleborough RUFC invites more girls to discover rugby as women's game continues to boom
articles.excerpt: Littleborough RUFC is inviting girls from Year 6 to under-18 level to try rugby this summer, as the sport continues to grow in popularity thanks to the success of England's Red Roses and increasing awareness of the physical and mental health benefits of team sport.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough Rugby Union Football Club is encouraging girls from across Rochdale borough to give rugby a try this summer, as participation in the women's and girls' game continues to grow at every level of the sport.

The club is holding open training sessions every Tuesday from 6pm until 7pm at its Rakewood Road ground in Littleborough, welcoming girls from Year 6 through to under-18 level. Organisers say there is no commitment required, with players of all abilities invited to come along, meet new friends and experience rugby in a supportive and inclusive environment.

The sessions are designed to introduce newcomers to the sport while allowing experienced players to develop their skills in a fun, welcoming atmosphere. Coaches are keen to stress that previous rugby experience is not necessary, with the emphasis firmly on enjoyment, teamwork and building confidence.

Over the past decade, girls' rugby has experienced remarkable growth across England. The Rugby Football Union has invested heavily in the women's and girls' game, with thousands more young people now playing regularly at schools and grassroots clubs. Many local clubs have expanded their junior girls' sections in response to increasing demand, creating more opportunities than ever before for young female players.

The sport has also benefited from the growing profile of the Red Roses, England's national women's rugby team. Consistently ranked among the best teams in the world, the Red Roses have inspired a new generation of players through their success on the international stage. Record-breaking attendances at Women's Six Nations matches and Rugby World Cup fixtures have demonstrated just how rapidly interest in women's rugby has grown, with elite players increasingly becoming role models for young girls considering taking up the sport.

That success at the highest level has filtered down into communities across the country. Grassroots clubs such as Littleborough RUFC have seen increasing interest from girls looking to get involved, whether for competition, fitness or simply to make new friends.

Beyond the physical benefits of exercise, rugby is widely recognised for the positive impact it can have on mental wellbeing. Taking part in team sports has been linked to reduced feelings of isolation, improved self-esteem and greater confidence, while the friendships formed through regular training and matches often provide valuable support networks for young people.

Coaches also point to the life skills rugby helps develop. Communication, resilience, leadership, discipline and respect for teammates and opponents are central values within the game, with many parents saying participation helps children grow in confidence both on and off the pitch.

The social aspect of rugby is another major attraction. Unlike many sports where players can feel under pressure from the outset, grassroots rugby clubs often place a strong emphasis on creating welcoming environments where everyone can progress at their own pace. That approach is reflected in Littleborough's message that all abilities are welcome and that there is no obligation to commit after attending a session.

The club hopes more girls from across Rochdale, Littleborough, Milnrow, Wardle and the surrounding communities will take the opportunity to experience the sport over the summer. Open training sessions allow newcomers to meet coaches and players, learn the basics and decide whether rugby is the right fit for them before the new season begins.

Training takes place every Tuesday between 6pm and 7pm at Littleborough RUFC, OL15 0AP. Girls in Year 6 through to under-18 level are invited to attend, with organisers encouraging anyone interested to simply come along and give it a go. For further information, prospective players or parents can contact Andy on 07990 744348.

As women's rugby continues to enjoy unprecedented growth across England, clubs such as Littleborough RUFC are hoping to inspire the next generation of players while demonstrating that the game offers far more than competition alone. For many young people, it can provide lasting friendships, improved wellbeing, greater confidence and the chance to become part of a thriving local sporting community.
